title: Building Reusable UI Systems
keywords: Professional Practices, Legacy Projects, and Further Learning
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Building Reusable UI Systems in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Building Reusable UI Systems within Professional Practices, Legacy Projects, and Further Learning. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Production work continues after the first successful render: teams need a reproducible workflow for review, upgrades, bug reports, and releases.

content_blocks.title: Building Reusable UI Systems: Component communication
content_blocks.alt_text: Component communication diagram for lesson 151: Building Reusable UI Systems. Parent owns the value or business intent → Child receives data and renders its view → Child emits intent; parent decides updates
content_blocks.caption: Component flow: data moves into children through props; emitted events communicate requested changes back to the owner.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Professional Vue engineering covers maintainable code, version control, documentation, migration, shared UI systems, and responsible community work. This lesson focuses on Building Reusable UI Systems. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Shared components and design tokens
items.text: For Shared components and design tokens, treat browser input and browser-held state as untrusted. Prefer Vue's escaped text interpolation for plain text, avoid compiling user-provided templates, and send authorization or sensitive decisions to a server that verifies them independently.

items.title: Component documentation
items.text: For Component documentation, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Theming and customization
items.text: For Theming and customization, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Packaging reusable components
items.text: For Packaging reusable components, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Versioning shared UI libraries
items.text: For Versioning shared UI libraries, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

content_blocks.code: Review the component API → remove duplicated logic → add behavior-focused checks → document setup and expected result.
content_blocks.expected_output: The process leaves a change that another developer can reproduce and review.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use the checklist on a small Vue component or project, then ask another person to follow the steps without additional context.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Building Reusable UI Systems with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Component documentation”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Professional Vue engineering covers maintainable code, version control, documentation, migration, shared UI systems, and responsible community work. For Building Reusable UI Systems, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Building Reusable UI Systems” that applies “Shared components and design tokens”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Shared components and design tokens”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
